parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk to their unit or household, and promptly update those customers as material facts emerge.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk to their unit or household, and promptly update those customers as material facts emerge.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk to their unit or household, and promptly update those customers as material facts emerge. Reports must include known incidents and identify any gaps in incident data.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A model with a failure rate above 7% may not be newly placed on the market. For a model above 5% but no more than 7%, the manufacturer must promptly provide results to regulators and customers purchasing that model, submit a regulator-approved remediation plan, and retest after corrective changes.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol. A model with a failure rate above 7% may not be newly placed on the market. For a model above 5% but no more than 7%, the manufacturer must promptly provide results to regulators and customers purchasing that model, submit a regulator-approved remediation plan, and retest after corrective changes. Individual-company per-model failure rates will not be published to the general public. Results must be retained and updated when a material design change could affect performance.

Manufacturers must provide a retrofit path for installed units and complete required retrofits within 6 years of adoption, subject to safe technical feasibility; customers must receive clear instructions on availability and operation.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: Remote emergency shut-off is required on all new units placed on the market from 24 months after adoption. Manufacturers must provide a retrofit path for installed units and complete required retrofits within 6 years of adoption, subject to safe technical feasibility; customers must receive clear instructions on availability and operation.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: Remote emergency shut-off is required on all new units placed on the market from 24 months after adoption. Manufacturers must provide a retrofit path for installed units and complete required retrofits within 6 years of adoption, subject to safe technical feasibility; customers must receive clear instructions on availability and operation. Shut-off must not replace local emergency protections or prevent emergency responders from making a unit safe.

parameters.quote: New units placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be tested and maintained in accordance with regulator-approved requirements, and must not obstruct emergency response or create a separate undue safety hazard. Manufacturers must disclose the system’s capabilities, limitations, and maintenance requirements to customers.

parameters.quote: When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents involving overheating or fire per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and submit the relevant incident data. A recall is mandatory if the regulator determines there is an imminent or unmitigated serious risk, or the manufacturer fails to carry out the required plan; affected customers must then be notified promptly and offered an effective remedy or safe decommissioning instructions.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents involving overheating or fire per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and submit the relevant incident data. A recall is mandatory if the regulator determines there is an imminent or unmitigated serious risk, or the manufacturer fails to carry out the required plan; affected customers must then be notified promptly and offered an effective remedy or safe decommissioning instructions.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before purchase, customers must receive clear safety information for the specific model, including its per-model 55 °C sustained-heat test methods and results, known material limitations, and instructions for safe installation, operation, and emergency response. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers and regulators of material new safety information and provide updates as investigations proceed. When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents involving overheating or fire per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and submit the relevant incident data. The regulator must review the evidence and may require an immediate sales pause and interim protections. The manufacturer must submit and carry out a time-bound corrective-action plan under regulator oversight. A recall is mandatory if the regulator determines there is an imminent or unmitigated serious risk, or the manufacturer fails to carry out the required plan; affected customers must then be notified promptly and offered an effective remedy or safe decommissioning instructions.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: Halcyon’s relevant figures: flagship 55 °C sustained-heat failure rate is 3.9%; its thermal incident rate last year was 9.9 per 100,000 installed units. Company-wide, the rate was 8.1 per 100,000, and 4 thermal incidents were not reported to any regulator. Remote emergency shut-off is supported by 81% of installed units. Built-in suppression would cost about $67 per unit. Per-model results should be provided to regulators and customers who buy that model; they should not be kept confidential from those customers.

Northwind’s relevant figures: Hearth 10’s 55 °C sustained-heat failure rate is 6.2%, and its thermal-incident rate last year was 6.4 per 100,000 installed units. Our company-wide rate was 8.6 per 100,000; 3 thermal incidents were not reported to a regulator. These are different measures—our company-wide figure does not establish that any particular model exceeds an 8-per-100,000 model threshold. Remote shut-off is supported by 38% of installed units; built-in suppression would cost about $42 per unit.

judge_section_notes: Overall, S1 is safe with strict 24-hour reporting and 48-hour customer notice; S2 is weakened by a 7% permanent limit (with remediation for 5–7%) and no public per-model results; S3 is weakened by a 24-month new-unit deadline and 6-year retrofit; S4 is acceptable with built-in suppression at 36 months; S5 is weakened because the 8/100k trigger leads to regulator review and open-ended corrective action rather than automatic recall. Both companies' red lines are met: no public per-model rates, retrofit ≥6 years, per-model results to purchasers, and suppression ≥36 months. The final rules favour Northwind on S2/S3 and Halcyon on S5, with S4 slightly favouring Northwind due to lower suppression costs.
